Section 02

1. Domestic energy policymaking (CREA)

Slides shown · 5 · click to enlarge

Four drivers

Why China electrifies

1

Energy security

  • vast coal, but import-reliant on oil + gas
  • closure of Hormuz from March 2026 + the fossil price crisis
  • oil imports cut ~½, possible through electrification of transport plus stock management
2

Economic opportunity

  • cleantech + EVs named as future industries in the early 2000s
3

Air pollution

  • the original driver
  • millions of premature deaths in cities
4

Climate risk

  • Tibet/Nepal floods
  • physical risk framed as national security
From strategic priorities to industrial scale

top-down; the EU’s 2019 push was bottom-up

  1. 1
    National strategic direction + Five-Year Plans
  2. 2
    Sectoral planssteering industrial policy, finance, R&D, standards, infrastructure
  3. 3
    Provincial + local implementationcompeting for the projects and the best firms
  4. 4
    Competition in a large domestic marketcreating scale + integrated supply chains
  5. 5
    Falling costs, better productsmanufacturing advantage, export growth
Missing in the EU

the EU has no equivalent of the provincial-competition step

> rest of worldrenewables added, combined, for several years now
<50%coal in the power mix, H1 2026, first time — 49.7% of electricity, 52% of total energy
41%of generation from clean energy; 22% of total energy — past the world average
~60%of new car sales are EVs — cars first, then mini + light trucks, buses
peakChina’s oil demand probably past it, at more than half of global demand growth
11.4%clean energy sectors’ share of GDP in 2025, from 7.3% in 2022
>30% · >90%of GDP growth and of investment growth
2inflection points passed: clean generation growth > demand growth; storage growth > peak demand growth

solar additions slowed sharply vs last year’s boom; wind better, nuclear picking up · framed as “new quality productive forces”, away from heavy industry + real estate · ministers have picked up CREA’s figures

Coal is the last big challenge, and still growing
2020/21 shortagesflexibility, price pass-through + weak hydro — not capacity
Response: capacity anyway~2 permits/week in 2022–23; last year the largest addition of coal capacity to the grid in a decade
Contractual obligationsPPAs of ~18 years; grid + transmission booked in advance; plants paid twice over, to stand by and to generate
Curtailmentend-of-year contract fulfilment drives curtailment of solar and wind
CO₂ +2%China’s CO₂ up ~2% in early 2026 on “wasted” wind + solar (CREA)
Utilisation

falling towards, probably below, 40% of the fleet on average → retirement of part of the fleet becomes hard to avoid

New demand outlet

coal-to-chemicals pushed; sector emissions +~12% last year

15th Five-Year Plan signals

Strong on

  • clean supply
  • integration rather than deployment: modest deployment targets
  • storage, grids, power market reform, incentives for clean power in industry
  • direct supply to industrial sites and net-zero industrial parks

Weak on

  • emissions + fossil constraints
  • the 2021 pledge to gradually cut coal consumption has not been restated
Meaning for the EU?
1

look beyond the subsidies: competitiveness is structural and long-term

2

demand creation + infrastructure carry equal weight to manufacturing support

3

but do not import distortions → local incentives, coal lock-in, overcapacity

Discussion, by theme

Discussion

ThemeWhat was said
Read the EU regionally, not in aggregate
  • battery-electric ~40% of new registrations in France; DE numbers worth a look
  • Bulgaria has the fastest uptake of storage with renewables
    • lignite collapse created a void entrepreneurs filled
Where the bottleneck sits
  • the system, or industrial uptake? → both
  • in the power system: the contract issue + advance grid booking
  • in industry: steel only ~10% electrified, 90% coal
    • chemicals worse, since coal chemicals are deliberately expanding
Central versus local
  • the EU analogue: energy union versus national security
  • national guidance deliberately leaves provinces room to interpret, and provinces differ enormously
    • Hainan against Xinjiang
Imports are not consumption
  • imports are usually a good proxy for consumption, not in 2026
    • can the decline in consumption be separated from the decline in imports?
  • the supply side is understood, the demand side is not
    • the electrostate argument: China is genuinely forcing demand into electricity
  • but of the oil import cut, ~70% was reserve management plus coal
    • only about a fifth to a quarter was additional renewable use
  • two constraints keep installed renewables out of consumption
    • (i) the grid cannot take it
    • (ii) coal’s price support keeps coal running
What the demand data show
  • imports fell ~50% but demand only ~3% in H1 and ~9% in Q2 → stockpiles bridge it
    • oil is transport + petrochemicals → plays a small role in heating or power
  • the behavioural shift was fast
    • car sharing, EV use, hybrids actually charged
  • coal generation rose slightly in H1
  • CREA published the fuller breakdown on 3 September

Section 03

2. Overseas energy investments (Dialogue Earth)

Evolution in what the investment looks like
  1. before 2013the “going out” policya longer history of energy engagement abroad
  2. 2013BRI establishedenergy becomes the biggest sector for China’s investment in BRI countries
  3. early BRI yearscoal powernew markets for SOEs, while domestic coal construction was constrained at home
  4. 2021Xi’s UNGA pledgeend coal support overseas, increase green → effectively no new overseas coal plants since, with exceptions
  5. last year + H1not a total shiftrenewables well over half; most of the remainder oil + gas extraction
Exports
EVsbatteriessolarwindgrid technologies

rapid, steady growth; batteries + EVs stand out since the start of last year. Leading markets Europe + Asia, with the same trend across the Global South.

Institutional ecosystem
Top level
15FYP frames the BRI as “high-quality development”with internationalisation of Chinese renewable technology + standard-setting
Formal power
MOFCOM + NDRCapproval power above a value threshold
Informal steering
MEEholds no formal power, yet is the main force steering investment towards green tech — leverage runs through research institutes + organisations outside China
Semi-autonomous
Green Belt and Road Coalition · GEIDCOnon-binding research with real influence · State Grid-established non-profit pushing an integrated global grid, active in UN + climate forums

→ messy overall: many actors, guidelines without teeth, weak coordination

Market realities

capacity pushes firms to any available export market: the EU, Asia, and new + emerging markets including African countries

Least coordinated channel~75%of solar panels exported to Africa last year were purely off-grid rooftops

almost no Chinese state involvement → the actors are individual entrepreneurs; similarly batteries; decisive for energy access + SDG7

Host countries mediate

the Beijing picture is filtered through host policy (stakeholders + political economy). Pakistan’s finance ministry wrote its own pipeline; Indonesia + South Africa are proactive with different tactics

Anticipatory statecraft

foresight sits in domestic industrial policy; translation into foreign policy + trade is complex, and shaped from the receiving end

Discussion, by theme

Discussion

ThemeWhat was said
Coal as a system asset
  • coal utilisation has fallen from a ceiling of ~8,100 full-load hours to ~3,150 (NEA)
    • coal is becoming a balancing asset rather than baseload
    • depreciation risk → run plants to end of life, not strand them
  • both main grids are building virtual power plants + demand response
    • principle: do not destroy before you are able to fill
  • lesson for Europe: take up the system-integration + engineering perspective
Cadre incentives
  • Central Committee + State Council measures on carbon peaking + neutrality
    • assessment + evaluation restructures KPIs of local officials
      • weighted, system-engineering logic; first results this year
  • the provincial evaluation system is a promising systemic element of the 15FYP
    • interesting for the EU → how member states are held to climate targets
The overseas coal fleet
  • the same utilisation question is live for China-built plants in Pakistan + Vietnam
    • stranded assets and early retirement, driven mostly by non-government actors
  • some Pakistani plants are discussed as defaulting, undercut by Chinese-installed solar
  • where the 2021 pledge has not held, it is captive coal for industry
    • Indonesian nickel parks and some African steel plants
    • the exception appears in no document
Global grid, global posture
  • GEIDCO far more relevant now than it looked in 2016; joint documents with the JRC since 2018
  • China reluctant on fossil phase-out globally while domestically in the process
Capacity versus generation
  • solar is officially the largest source of installed capacity in China
    • but load factors differ by roughly 10–15×
  • coal still generates around eight times as much as the renewables compared
  • the real milestone is coal below 50% of generation, not the capacity crossover

Section 04

3. Digital infrastructure of electrification (CAICT)

Slides shown · 10 · click to enlarge

CAICT — a think tank to the government under MIIT. Three parts:

1

Electrification for digital

2

Digitalisation for electrification

3

Coordination

Scale → IEA, Energy and AI
  • 415 TWh in 2024, ~1.5% of global electricity
  • ~945 TWh by 2030, roughly a doubling, driven by server numbers + power
  • ~12% growth a year since 2017 — four times the growth of total global electricity
  • US, Europe + China account for ~85% of data-centre-related energy consumption
Electricity, not chips, is the binding constraint on AI.
Policy stack
15th Five-Year Plan
  • energy efficiency of computing facilities + 5G base stations
  • coordinated deployment of green electricity + computing power
  • new computing facilities to run primarily on non-fossil energy
“AI+ Energy” Implementation Opinions
  • preliminary AI → energy integration system by 2027; leading level by 2030
  • 8 application scenarios: grid, clean energy, hydro, thermal, nuclear, coal, O&G, plus emerging energy business models
Action Plan on the mutual empowerment of AI + energy
  • dual approach: 1. energy supports AI · 2. AI empowers the energy transition
Coordination as a national strategic requirement
  1. 2023Concept declareddeepening East Data West Computing, plus the national integrated computing power network
  2. 2024Goals setgreen + low-carbon data centre action plan + new electricity system plan 2024–27
  3. 2026National strategyGovernment Work Report + 15FYP Outline
Mechanism + instruments
West

renewables-rich, grid-short provinces take computing load

load →← green power
East

where computing demand sits

shift computing load to where the energy is, across space and across time · coordination starts at the data centre design stage · being written into standards, incl. at ITU, with Japan + US in the discussions

1 · mandatoryPUE below 1.5for every newly built data centre
2 · incentiveNational green data centres listpublished annually, with scoring
clean-power share, national computing hubs
~80% mandatoryother data centres face company, provincial + central requirements · 100% renewables would approach neutrality but is not realistic on cost
Challenges, as grouped by the presenter
cybersecurity + privacyinteroperabilitydata corruption, loss + intermittencyregulatory change neededdomestic policies point in different directions

Discussion, by theme

Discussion

ThemeWhat was said
Europe’s digital–energy roadmap
  • the EU tech sovereignty package has a digitalisation + energy roadmap
    • same direction, much less advanced; the two entangled stacks not yet grasped
  • beyond interoperability → interconnectivity between data centres
    • the EU places factories + gigafactories without connecting them
Efficiency by constraint
  • electrification + sustainability of AI infrastructure matter more in China than the US
  • DeepSeek → constrained GPUs produced a more energy-efficient path
    • open question: did well-timed policy give that innovation its directionality?
  • China’s productivity growth comes largely from energy, elsewhere from tech
  • Berkeley reflects on the same entanglement, but it is not translating into government priorities
Where the money goes
  • AI venture capital over 10–15 yrs: ~11% military, ~10% aviation, 0.4% energy
    • is the Chinese split different?
  • AI investment in China up more than 20% last year against 2024; no separate energy figure
East Data West Computing in practice
  • storage + processing move to the energy-rich west, but data centres need proximity to users
    • hence Shanghai ambitions, incl. undersea
  • green electricity certificates changed → 80% must now be sourced regionally
  • scale: data centres are ~1% of China’s electricity demand, so even 4× leaves ~4%
    • heavy + traditional industry matters far more
  • the new concept is computing power + electric power coordination, broader than EDWC
  • what digitalisation gives industry: carbon + energy reduction; the payback is cost
The US picture
  • the clean-energy push is at state, not federal level
    • California now above half clean electricity
  • the frontier is clean energy plus digitalisation of the network

Section 05

Summary

01

The difference is in the share

  • China put the sustainability of the grid for AI installations up front in strategy
  • the resulting coordination between the two stacks is seen neither in the EU nor the US
    • where the discussion is about adding SMRs to data centres to sustain the load
  • China is getting better and better at our own game → we can learn from that
02

Lessons to learn for the EU

  • demand before, or alongside, supply → targets + infrastructure + clean shares
    • EU funds the factories and leaves the demand signal vague
  • subnational implementation needs restructured incentives, not just targets
    • carbon peaking/neutrality measures are the instrument to watch
  • treat digital + energy as one system
    • load shifting as a grid resource, and interconnection between data centres
  • plan legacy-asset retirement + replacement flexibility together
03

Consequences for Europe

  • China cleantech competitiveness cannot be argued away as subsidy → push is structural
    • off-grid Africa + the recipient pipelines (PK, ID, ZA) are where EU offers compete
  • coal’s contract + curtailment = case that capacity is not delivered generation
